      I too was born and raised in California and never thought we had an accent.  However, when I was in the Marine Corps we were in Japan and one day on liberty a few of us went out to the local city.  
      In the restaurant we were in the (Japanese) waitress they sent over, when speaking to us, we could all hear that English was a first language for her.  
      After talking to our group for a while I eventually asked her if she was from California?  She said she was.  
      “Sacramento?”
      “Yeah.  How’d you know?”
      All the other Marines at the table asked me how I knew that.
      “I don’t know.”, I said.  “I could just hear Sacramento.”
      Trying to figure it out, a couple things I thought of where, I could be wrong, on words ending with “ing”, we have a tendency to drop the “g”.  And, for example, as Boston drops their “r”’s, we actually put an emphasis on pronouncing our “r”’s.
      I haven’t been in Sacramento in over twenty years so I don’t know how much, if anything, Sacramento has changed.

      I believe the term “pan out” came from prospectors panning for gold. They would collect soil in a grid pattern in an area they believed had a gold vein. They would pan the soil in the river or stream looking for traces of gold.       Hey, I'm not Brian, but I am brazilian and I can understand like 50-60% of spanish. Maybe I can help you somehow.
      
      1. First of all, Spanish people speak lotta fast. Like, really really fast, almost on a japanese level. So if you're not familiar with the flow of the language (basic sounds, how one sound connect to each other, etc), it'll be hard to understand. My advide would be: exposure. Listen to Spanish everyday, and if you have the opportunity, slow down the track you're hearing.
      
      2. If you struggle on vocabulary, Anki may help, but reading thing in Spanish also helps a lot. You can also try to express yourself in Spanish on your routine. Lemme explain: you see a red, beautiful car. Then, you ask yourself: how this would be said in Spanish? If you don't know, search it up.
      
      Hope I could help you!

    ↳ **@silvercrystal3** (👍1 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DEH2-WXjNwM&lc=UgwhV4pwS6HnHBziXGd4AaABAg.A5TTVaqdNZ_AGbNSgRVpqi
      hey coincidentally I'm a native German deep diving into japanese grammar for about 3 years by now - and yes, as someone diving really deep into the structure of both languages, the similarities between them indeed go so much deeper than any commonly known learning source actually tends to teach; this starts with syntax-related things like grammar cases (which is a totally foreign concept for most english speaking folks out there, hence you won't hear it being mentioned anywhere at all basically) and goes over literal transitions between phrases that actually end up in a kind of archaic 1:1-translation as it would have been in German, which overall can be somewhat hilarious once you start getting the hang of it - but you must be a rather literal thinker in order to get these connections and finding them out on your own.
      
      It's basically like reverse-engineering japanese into "Literal German", which is even a 'foreign' concept for native German folks since ppl speaking a language vs. grasping it structurally can easily be as much two different things as speaking two entirely different languages.

      BUT. 
      
      If i walk past a group of friends talking about how Jenny said with irony that Paul loved the movie. I'm gonna assume the irony is that he wouldn't have liked the movie, but loved it in the end. 
      
      However, if I walk past a group of friends and I hear Jenny said sarcastically that Paul loved the movie. Then I would say he DIDN'T love it.
      
      That's my real life comparison living in the U.S. 
      
      
      English being my second language, I've been in the U.S. since 8 yrs old. All my advanced English classes would only ever focus on 'irony' being part of a plot/story/circumstance. Not ever did I get taught a Webster's dictionary definition of what irony is. I learned sarcasm through social events. 
      
      So my brain, seeing this question, does NOT trigger the right answer. 
      
      I chose A, bcs of how I was taught what irony is. So Jenny, saying it "with a little more than irony", instantly made me think of scenarios where Paul would have hated this movie, but he ended up loving it. 
      
      I can tell you right now that unless the teacher had said: "with a little sarcasm". NO English native in my area would have guessed the correct answer because of how irony/sarcasm is used socially. (The definition isn't the law of language, multiple words over the years have gotten revisions on their definitions. This is why I think the way he used irony in a dictionary definition was okay, but sarcasm would have been the better socially accepted wording.) Let me know what you guys think. TY :)
    ↳ **@Puma5** (👍4 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J09NUmXEJuY&lc=Ugxc-QSx7yNqbqMtACx4AaABAg.AAGlWfUPJtmACOkxmQ2HbK
      Not in the English language it’s not. Irony is stating the opposite of what is actually true, often with a humorous twist or to express frustration. This is different to a situation defying expectations, e.g. ‚an irony of fate‘, or dramatic irony. 
      Sarcasm is one level up, it is using the opposite of what is meant but is generally more cutting, often used in a vitriolic way with the intention to slight or mock someone.

  As a Spanish learner, one thing my Dad (who is fluent in Spanish) recommended me to do once I started watching things in Spanish, which is one idea I do recommend to others if they perhaps struggle too much (at this moment in time) with native Spanish language content… watch a movie you’ve seen a million times in English (for me it would be Sam Raimi’s Spider-Man trilogy and the six Pre Disney Star Wars movies, for example) and watch them in the Spanish dub (whether it be Spain or Latin American Spanish dub depends on your goals) with Spanish subtitles, that way you can focus on the vocabulary and learning new phrases because you don’t need to feel lost on the general story. You can focus so much on the vocab spoken by the characters (or the ones on the subtitles when you just can’t make out what they are saying) and learn many new phrases from that. Over time, you can then build to native Spanish language content because you’ll have a more intensive vocabulary under your belt you recognize. Still, I’d say this trick works best for intermediate learners and up.

      Wow, you guys are all so cool! I am encouraged.
      
      I guess I’ll share an update. I’ve mostly focused on Japanese lately (since I’m half-Japanese) and every time I study, I see more and more how much there is to learning an additional language. It’s honestly overwhelming.
      
      I think the key however, is exactly the same anatomical mental process that one uses to get better at Chess. Masters of the game study thousands of games played by the best in history, and as such, they begin to recognize patterns in their own games. They find themselves in situations that they cal recall. So by taking the same approach to language, where I prioritize repetition over intentional memory, I can get better simply by going through the motions and I will naturally get better.
      
      I have found European languages to be a hell of a lot easier too, just because they all have much more in common with English than Japanese. What a surprise, right?
      
      I think actually learning those languages will be easier after I become relatively fluent in Japanese, but we’ll see.
      
      As far as Arabic goes, I know there are numerous Arabic speakers in this channel’s subscriber base, but me personally, I haven’t had much interest in learning it. At least, not right now. My mind may change in the future, but Japanese is my main focus, then later, Mandarin and those European languages. After that, I will consider Arabic or perhaps other languages. Cheers! :)
    ↳ **@QoheletMentorship** (👍0 · 2026-05-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SVS8swDuJ_4&lc=UgxLMmMZv4JejShc49N4AaABAg.A7VWwnnkRorAVqdEBOIxBL
      Update for y'all, I'm scholastically studying Japanese now both as a class and in the form of tadoku , or "many reading" in Japanese. It's pretty overwhelming to suddenly be thrust into an environment where a new language smothers your surroundings, but over time, I noticed that I see the same words being used in different places and they help me not only figure out what they mean, but also to remember them better.
      
      In fact, just today, I saw the word 道 \michi\, meaning 'road' or 'street,' which is what I learned initially. When I saw it used today when reading a manga however, it was referring to animal tracks. Seeing that same word again used elsewhere is what helped me remember that so well.

  The break from learning and reactivitaion effectiveness was covered in golden list method. 
  The principle is, there is short term memmory, temporal memory, long term memory.
  Temporal memory is about two weeks recession. 
  The ones you recall after two weeks are in long term memmory. You will at least recognize the word but might not recall at request. 
  Method plays it by learning stuff and noting down stuff. Then after 2 weeks see what you dont know in notes, you write down what you didnt, repeat.
  
  So you switch two exercise books 2 weekly. Something like that.

  I'm learning 4 languages right now. I am conversationally fluent in Japanese, been learning it for 4 years. The other 3 are very recent. I maintain my Japanese by listening to podcasts and speaking to natives on calls. I'm advancing my Chinese right now, it's the only one I wish to take formal language exams in the future. Then Greek for only 15 minutes a day, I treat it casually. Arabic for 30 minutes, focusing on Fusha this year then Hijazi next year. I separate them like this; anime and podcasts for japanese, c dramas and textbooks for mandarin. Then I speak with AI to practice Greek and Arabic. In a day I only do 2 and repeat the cycle eg if today I did Chinese and Arabic tomorrow it's Japanese and Greek. It reduced a lot of cognitive overload as it gets tiring to do 4 languages in a day. I agree with the personality point as well. Even things like music shouldn't be mixed up.

  I have done this for Tibetan and Kannada. I delibarately chose different language families so they don't mix in my head. You should keep in mind that the language is only one component of your study. You're also learning the culture, facts about the national character of the speakers, and about the literature of that language, which could be huge. This literature informs the language you're learning with idioms, turns of phrase, and so on. The deeper you get into this ocean, the deeper it gets. There is also the issue with dialects - some of them can be quite distinct from eachother and have literature written in them that might also be huge.

      我今天下午去你家吃饭
      我今天下午吃饭去你家
      我吃饭今天下午去你家
      今天下午吃饭我去你家

      私は日本人なのでこの人の評価が正当かどうかの判断できないけど､個人としては概ね同意。
      語順が決まっていない文法だったり使う文字の種類が尋常じゃなかったり句点を使わなかったり。どれも初見では最高級に理解ができないけど､受け入れることができてしまえばあとは簡単。
      多少の違和感はあっても文法は間違うことがないから伝わってくれる。日常会話だけ見たら最も簡単な言語の1つに数えられてもいいんじゃないかとすら思う。読み書きには漢字を使っていて更に日本昔ながらの独自の仮名をたくさん使うから結構難しい。でも文字から発音がわかりやすいし漢字も話してみると結構身につくと思う。
      ここまで聞くとむしろ見た目のとっつきにくさ以外に最も難しい言語と言われる筋合いが無いんじゃないか､と思えてくるだろう？
      
      ⋯⋯しかしそれは間違いだと私は思う。ここまで書いた話は､日本語ネイティブになるための目線ではなく外国人が日本で生活できるかっていう目線だった。
      厳密にそこそこ正しくて社会的に普通の日本人として通用するレベルの日本語を話したり書いたりするっていうのは､とんでもなく至難の業だ。さっきまでは見掛け倒しとして紹介した､独特の文法だったり漢字の読み書きだったりが牙を剥いてくる。軽くアニメを見ながら勉強しつつで6年程度を暮らすだけとかだと一朝一夕に身についたりしない。その2つを比べると本当にレベルの桁が違うと思う。
      私はアラビア語圏に行ったことがないのでアラビア語にはそれほど詳しくないけど､ネイティブになるって条件ならば根拠なしに間違いなく一番難しい言語。だけど普通に話すだけなら大抵の場合相手が日本語ネイティブだから文意を読み取ってくれるそのおかげで見掛けの割にはかなり簡単な言語。と言えるような印象だな
      
      言語はそのままその国に結びつくから､
      ネイティブになるためには日本の色んな時代や色んな国が絡んだ複雑な歴史と長年の島国暮らしの風習だったりをなんとなく理解しないといけないので､日本生まれじゃないネイティブはめっちゃめっちゃ凄いと思っている。

    ↳ **@oliver_peng** (👍12 · 2025-10-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m6TS9G1XEj0&lc=UgzeG9EDt5nUYsnbQsd4AaABAg.A3l9o0K7DruANzR2bZNwMI
      Yes, 100% agree. This is exactly what other commenters mean when they say Japanese gets harder the further you go. There’s a huge gap between being understandable and sounding truly native. And while saying “that's true for all languages” isn't wrong, it misses the point. What we’re talking about is the size of that gap COMPARED to other languages.
      
      I can’t speak for Arabic, but if the metric for difficulty is how much time and effort it takes to convincingly pass as a native speaker, my experience is that far more learners can pass as native in Mandarin than in Japanese—at least over the course of a one-minute conversation. It’s true that Japanese pronunciation is “easy” if the only goal is to be understood, which is a fairly low bar. “Moo-cho gratch-ee-us” or “Bon-jerrr” are perfectly understandable, after all. The deceiving accessibility of Japanese causes many learners underestimate the importance of pitch accent in Japanese (many students and teachers completely ignoring the topic), and that’s usually the giveaway. I’ve rarely met a learner whose accent wasn’t immediately noticeable.
      
      Another area that was glossed over is keigo. Between sonkeigo/kenjōgo, teineigo, and tameguchi, it’s almost like navigating three different languages. Knowing which level of politeness to use in a given context takes years of immersion; studying alone won’t get you there. Are you talking to a child? A stranger’s child? A teacher? A teacher who’s now a colleague? A close friend who’s also your senior at work? A friend whose closeness is a bit ambiguous? A co-worker that's older than you but lower in the workplace hierarchy? A family member? Mother-in-law? Son-in-law? Japanese politeness levels aren’t just about “formal vs. casual,” but about social distance, hierarchy, and context. There’s no single “right” answer for every situation and sometimes you need to adjust as relationships evolve.
      
      There are also distinct masculine and feminine speech patterns in Japanese, and since most teachers are women, many learners end up sounding unintentionally feminine. Developing a natural sense for what’s gender-appropriate takes a lot of time and exposure.
      
      Japanese also poses unique challenges because it borrowed Chinese characters but discarded tones, resulting in a huge number of homophones. People pointed out that characters like 生 or 日 can have dozens/hundreds of pronunciations, but I think the bigger issue is that a single pronunciation can correspond to many different meanings. For example, “senzai” can mean detergent, potentiality, pre-existence, garden, millennium, advertising material, decoration, or wire. “Kenshō” could refer to inspection, a palace sanctuary, a charter, honoring, awarding a prize, good health, spirit, swordsmithing, self-awareness, revealing the truth, and more. The intended meaning is usually obvious from context, but it can still make learning new vocabulary maddening—especially as your vocabulary expands. “Another kenshō? Seriously...?”
      
      The one area that made Japanese easier, though, is access to material. Thanks to the sheer volume of video games, anime, manga, and films available today and the explosion of learning resources over the past decade, learners now have unprecedented ways to immerse themselves in the language.

      @starpeep5769  I also watch Japanese NHK Taiga dramas, and in Japanese period dramas, the language only changes in terms of sentence endings. Once you learn a few of these endings, anyone who understands modern Japanese can follow along. In contrast, Chinese historical dramas often use four-character idioms or classical Chinese even in key parts of the story, making it hard to follow without knowing them. 
      In China, using four-character idioms is considered cool, and honestly, I hear them every day. While Japan also has four-character idioms and proverbes, they are rarely used in daily conversation, and you certainly don’t hear them every day. Japanese government public relations documents use standard modern Japanese, but in China, government documents are preferred to be more literary, often incorporating historical allusions and four-character idioms. Even at the United Nations, Chinese representatives often use four-character idioms in their speeches, and I always think it must be tough for the interpreters to translate those into English in real time.

      @marwaqoura7804  Yeah, Greek is the hardest Western language to learn. On the other hand, Slavic languages are much easier, and they all have lots of similarity between them (for example, I can understand a tiny bit of Slovenian and a fair bit of Bulgarian even though I've never learned those languages nor ever stepped a foot in those countries, simply because of how many words they share with my mother tongue, Bosnian).
      
      I knew a guy who was 18 last year and he could read and write in at least 11 languages (could be more, but I've personally witnessed him conversing with people in those 11 languages).. although he can only speak 3 or 4 of them fluently (Arabic, German and English afaik). The other languages he knows on a basic level are: Mandarin (he can read and write it, so Idk if that counts as basic), Korean, Japanese, Hebrew, Assyrian, Greek, Latin, and Persian. He learned Greek and Latin at school, and all other languages he learned on his own (and for German, the way he became fluent was he had a book which was half in English half in German (alternating pages) and by reading that his comprehension became fluent, then he started speaking with people at some point too). He's a really humble guy, he did not consider himself a polyglot at all, he said he doesn't consider basic skills in a language to count towards being a polyglot, and I'm not even sure if he knows more languages, since he never went around telling people the languages he knows, I just kept a note of the languages I saw him use (this was on discord).
      
      Fun fact, he's the one who made me learn hiragana when I said I don't want to learn how to read Japanese, just speak it (I learned it with him over two weeks; I'd first do about 5 kanji every day on an app and then later on that night he would give me practice sentences to read).. and what's even crazier is that he was using Arabic to teach me Japanese (so basically two non-Arabs speaking Arabic while learning Japanese, crazy isn't it). That worked since we're both fluent in Arabic.. we talked in fus7a though because we both wanted to improve on it, and people kept on wondering why we're not using an dialect 😂but we just kept going and eventually I did learn to read Japanese.. he was an interesting guy

  Present simple - fact habit and schedule 
  Present Continuous - Right now
  Present Perfect - Action from past describes anything now ( Experience ) 
  Present Perfect Continuous - Action from the past never stopped, on going action
  
  Past Simple - An action started in the past and finished in the past
  Past Continuous - An action continued from past but we give context to another thing 
  Past Perfect - Always come before an action
  Past Perfect Continuous - Describes an action that continued over time when another action was done
  Future Simple - Talk about action will happen in the future 
  Future Continuous - Talk about the action that will continue over a period of time in the future 
  Future Perfect - Talk about action that will finish by a certain time in the future
  Future Perfect Continuous - Talking about a continuous action that will finish that will be completed at a given time in future

      ​ @2narXeyyam "concur WITH" what you said. Not concur in.
      You use "with", or "in". Never "to" after concur.
      "I concur with him". Speaks to you agreeing with him
      "I concur in his verdict"
      However your use of "to" is correct with "agree": "I agree to that". Agreeing to an action. Or "I agree with that." ie "I concur"!
      I hope that helps

      ​ @MarcusVinicius-ho2li    OK, the reason loads of people here are commenting the same – that completing C1/C2 but getting answers for the lower levels wrong doesn't make sense (and they're right) is that 1, there are only a few questions for each level and 2, the CEFR is way more complex than that. 
      Also, we all pick up bits of language when the situation is right, and we're all different. There's a theory that we learn stuff in the “order of acquisition”, and generally we often do, but it's very often that we don't! Here's an example: I asked my daughter, at age 3, if she wanted an afternoon snack and replied “No, Daddy, I've already eaten.” Present perfect!? 🤯 Amazing, right! 
      Well, not really. She'd heard people in the family using that structure 100s of times (and internalised it). So, in the right situation (where she needed it), it just came out. Clearly, she took no notice of the Order of Acquisition! 😂
      
      For more on the CEFR / anything language learning. DM @personallanguagetrainer on Instagram, happy to help!

  I’m learning Arabic in USA. Here’s a helpful method I developed.
  I decided to first learn common thought strings and ‘think’ in Arabic. Day 1 of learning, If I’m hungry I think “I am hungry” in Arabic. Day 2 “I am hungry, I want x” with my thoughts becoming slightly more complicated each day. Same for bathroom and sleep and all basic functions. It’s been extremely effective to the point I now believe I could learn a variety of languages. Try it out, or develop your own system that works for you, but make sure you have a system you LIKE that’s fun. Don’t get discouraged, and don’t try to learn too much at once.

  I really love when I see a non-Arabic trying to speak, let alone teach, the language to others, even if the pronunciation is not as the native (which is normal).. Keep it up.
  
  Just a really very small correction, yet very important: in the minute 9:28 about the reply to the greeting, you pronounce it correctly but it's not written correctly (in Arabic).
  It should be "و عليكم السلام" not "و عليكم السام",  (just the letter "ل" was missing), as the meaning will change from "Peace" to "Boredom".
  
  "And upon you be boredom" is the written reply.
  
  I know it was done by mistake and not intentional, but still it's always good to correct ourselves and to have people around us that help us to be better.
  
  Once again, keep it up, you're one of a few.

      ​​ @Xy33zr  I strongly disagree with this. If your goal is to speak with people, why not just learn to speak with people in the language they actually use? 
      
      Sure, learning MSA makes learning a dialect easier, but learning ANY variety of Arabic makes learning any other easier. Again, might as well start with something people actually speak. 
      
      That's like saying you should learn Latin before Spanish or french. Just starting with Spanish will probably be more efficient. 
      
      Your English is very impressive of course, but no language is "proper". The best way to talk to people is to talk to them in their language. Not the language of books from hundreds of years ago. Those aren't reflective of the language of the current age.

      @Xy33zr  Of course it all depends on your goals definitely. It's just that people don't speak MSA in daily life. So yes, everyone in the Arab world can understand you with MSA, it simply isn't the most practical if you're trying to use Arabic. 
      
      I actually see most people recommend starting with a major dialect because it gets you access to speaking partners immediately in a language that can be used in daily conversation. 
      
      It's important to remember that Arabic dialects are very different, almost like different languages. You might want to speak to everyone, but I don't think that's really that important. If you learn any language you always need to make the choice of what people you want to talk to. In other words, you can learn MSA and technically talk to everyone in a dialect no one speaks daily, or, speak to less people but in a language that's actually used. 
      
      I will always recommend just picking a dialect because it's basically the same as picking a language. If it's Egyptian, you even get all the benefits of learning MSA too. (Everyone can understand you in the Arab world, and it makes learning other dialects, even MSA, easier)

**@ShoroqAlahmady** (👍0 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IsvuOoaKiAM&lc=UgxozY_DN_i-5imes6x4AaABAg
  وكذلك أنتم يا معشر النّصارى آمِنوا بالحقّ مُصدِّقاً لما معكم من قبل أن يطمِس الله على وجوه قلوبكم فيرُدّها على أدبارها فتكفروا بالمسيح الحقّ وهو يدعوكم إلى الإسلام واتّباع المهديّ المنتظَر، ويكفر بعقيدتكم الباطل يا معشر النّصارى فيقول: إنّه عبدٌ لله ولم يكنِ الله ولا ولد الله، فيتبرّأ منكم بسبب شِركِكُم والمبالغة في نبيّكم بغير الحقّ فيدعوكم إلى الحقّ، فإذا لم تجيبوا داعي الحقّ فيطمس الله على قلوبكم فيردّها على أدبارها فتكفرون بالمسيح عيسى ابن مريم عليه الصلاة والسلام فتتّبعون المسيح عيسى ابن مريم الكذاب، ولم يكن ابن مريم بل هو كذاب لذلك يُسمّى المسيح الكذاب، أم تظنون يا معشر المسلمين أنّ المسيح الكذاب سوف يأتي فيقول: "أنا المسيح الكذّاب" فيفضح نفسه؟! بل سوف يقول: "أنا المسيح عيسى ابن مريم وأنا الله ربّ العالمين". لعنه الله.. وقال لأتّخِذَنّ من عبادك نصيبًا مفروضًا، إنّه الشيطان الرجيم بذاته والله على ما أقول شهيد ووكيل، فيتّبعه المشركون من النّصارى ظنّاً منهم إنّه المسيح عيسى ابن مريم الحقّ لأنّه وافق عقيدتهم في ابن مريم بغير الحقّ وقال إنّه الله ربّ العالمين.
  
  ولسوف أنَبِئُكُم كيف تُميّزون بين الحقّ والباطل وذلك لأنّ المسيح الحقّ يقول للناس ما قاله وهو في المهد صبيًّا: {قَالَ إِنِّي عَبْدُ اللَّـهِ آتَانِيَ الْكِتَابَ وَجَعَلَنِي نَبِيًّا ﴿٣٠﴾} صدق الله العظيم [مريم]، ويقول إنّه عبد لله ويحاجِج النّصارى في عقيدة الباطل فلا يُعجِب المجرمون قوله فيُكذّبونه.
  
  فأمّا شياطين البشر من اليهود فيكونون من أوّل التابعين وهم يعلمون إنّه الشيطان الرجيم وإنّه ليس المسيح عيسى ابن مريم عليه الصلاة والسلام؛ بل يعلمون إنّه الطاغوت الذي هم له عابدون، وشياطين البشر من اليهود يريدون أن يُضِلوا النّصارى والمسلمين عن الصراط المستقيم فيكونوا سواءً معهم في أصحاب السعير ذلك لأنّهم يئِسوا من رحمة الله كما يئِس الكفّار من أصحاب القبور.
  
  ويا معشر النّصارى لا تتّبعوا قومًا ضلّوا وأضلّوا كثيرًا وهم يعلمون، وأنا المهديّ المنتظَر النّاصر للمسيح عيسى ابن مريم عليه الصلاة والسلام، والنّاصر لما جاء به محمّدٌ رسول الله صلّى الله عليه وآله وسلّم، فمن كان من أنصار محمّد رسول الله والمسيح عيسى ابن مريم فهو من المسلمين، ونحن المسلمون نُصدِّق بالإسلام الذي جاء به المسيح عيسى ابن مريم عليه الصلاة والسلام وكذلك جاء به من بعده محمدٌ رسول الله صلّى الله عليه وآله وسلّم، وإنّ الدّين عند الله الإسلام ومن ابتغى غير الإسلام دينًا فلن يُقبَل منه وهو في الآخرة لمن الخاسرين.
  
  وأنا المهديّ المنتظَر المؤمن بحبيبي المسيح عيسى ابن مريم، والمؤمن بجدّي وحبيبي محمّد رسول الله صلّى الله عليه وآله وسلّم، ولربّما يود أحد المتابعين للحقّ أن يقول: "وما خطبك لا تذكر موسى؟ ألِأنّ طائفة اليهود يَدينون بدين موسى؟". فنقول: بل دينُ موسى عليه الصّلاة والسّلام هو الإسلام دين إبراهيم وإسماعيل ويعقوب ويوسف، ولكن اليهود يدينون بدين الطاغوت ولا يتّبعون رسول الله موسى فهم له كارهون كما يكرهون المسيح عيسى ابن مريم الحقّ، وكما يكرهون محمداً رسول الله صلّى الله عليه وآله وسلّم. وأرى بعض علماء الأمّة الجاهلين يسمّون بعض طوائف اليهود مُتطرّفين وكأنّهم لموسى مُخلصِين؛ بل تطرّفهم من شدّة إخلاصهم لربِّهم الطاغوت الشيطان الرجيم فتجدونهم من ألدّ الخصام لله ولرسله وللمؤمنين، ولكنّ أكثر النّاس لا يعلمون.. وسلامٌ على المُرسَلين، والحمد لله ربّ العالمين.

  Great tips! Here's what I'd add based on what worked for me:
  
  Vocabulary: Duolingo ✅ (you mentioned this)
  Grammar: YouTube tutorials like this ✅
  Pronunciation diagnosis:** Pronounce Lab (2-min free test)
  Listening: Podcasts and Netflix ✅
  Conversation: iTalki or HelloTalk
  
  The pronunciation step is what most people skip. You learn 5,000 words but don't know how to say them correctly.
  
  I wasted 6 months doing "conversation practice" without knowing my weak sounds. Once I took a pronunciation assessment and saw TH = 65%, I practiced that for 2 weeks and got way more improvement than 6 months of generic practice.
  
  Moral: Use specialized tools for each skill, don't rely on one method for everything.

  you have done a great job explaining the Arabic language but there is one thing : the noun "dogs" "كلاب" is not a feminine noun. it's called "جمع تكسير" 
  It is treated as the singular feminine in reference like we say : الكلاب تطارد" اللصوص"
  وهذا شرح بسيط: "الكلاب" لفظ مذكر لكنه جمع تكسير لغير العاقل، وهذا النوع من الجموع يعامل معاملة المفرد المؤنث في الإشارة والوصف وعودة الضمير... فتقول مثلًا: هذه كلاب مدرّبة، والكلاب تطارد اللصوص. وهذه الكلاب سائبة.

  The plural in Arabic is not limited to masculine and feminine. There is a sound masculine plural, a sound feminine plural, and a broken plural(Yeah,that is its official name), which is anything that is neither masculine (does not end with the letters “-ون” or “-ين”) nor feminine (does not end with the letters “-ات”) and is an irregular and unexpected plural.

  I am from United Arab Emirates and my mother tongue is Arabic, i would like to note that your last point regarding plural form is not correct as we have 4 types of plural forms جمع مذكر سالم ، جمع مؤنث سالم ، جمع تكسير ، جمع الجمع which are masculine plural, feminine plural, broken plural and plural of a plural which and each is used depending on the word itself and the context of the sentence. The plural of a dog you used is actually masculine plural while the feminine plural would be كلبات as the word singular form is actually masculine. An example of a plural of a plural is used when you want to combine more than two sets of groups under one word like رجال is a plural but in one country you have for example military men and police men and firemen but they are all combined to be men of one country so you can use the word رجالات which is “grammatically” considered feminine although you are literally combining a masculine plural with a masculine plural. This is very pro level Arabic but i hope my comment helped you understand and deepen your Arabic language learning more and i am sure this would be helpful even for 90% of native Arabs as well

Colloquial Egyptian Arabic is great for communication among Arabs, social media, and understanding Egyptian movies, etc. But at the end of the day, teaching Arabic requires mastering Arabic grammar.   The rule is simple. Whatever you're exposed to will eventually manifest.

  عاوز أقولك حاجة يا براين ... 
  
  لازم تعرف أن هناك فرق من الفروق الكبيرة في العربية والأنجليزية أيضاً ...
  
  ** أن هناك الجملة الإسمية والجملة الفعلية .. 
  مفيش في اللغة الإنجليزية إلا جملة فعلية فقط .. 
  أما اللغة العربية ففيها الجملة الإسمية : التي تبدأ بإسم . وتتكون من ( مبتدأ + خبر ) 
  المبتدأ : الشمس . 
  الخبر : مشرقة . 
  الشمس مشرقة .. 
  
  والجملة الإسمية تبدأ : بمبتدأ وخبر . والخبر إما ( مفرد - جملة - شبة جملة ) 
  
  يعني في فروق كتيرة . يا عزيزي .
  وكمان : من ضمن الفروق !!
  أن اللغة العربية تمتاز بــ : 
  لغة الضد ( ض ) ليس هناك أي لغة بها حرف الضاد ( ض ) .
  بها أدوات النداء :  ( يا - أيا - الهمزة [ ء ] ) أدوات النداء بها ثلاثة .
  بها أيضاً المثني المذكر والمثني المؤنث .
  بها أيضاً : الجملة الفعلية : وتتكون من ( فعل + فاعل + مفعول به ) أو صفة أو جار ومجرور . 
  
  اللغة العربية : بحرها كبير . ومش ممكن تنتهي بفيديو من 3 أو أربع دقائق .. ده لازم فيديو كبير .. جداً .. 
  
  شكراً لمجهودك .. ولازم تقرأ كويس عن اللغة العربية .. أتمني أن نتواصل مع بعض 
  في أفكار كتيرة ممكن نتواصل مع بعض . ممكن أعطيلك أفكار نعملها مع بعض في فيديوهات . وممكن نعمل حاجة كويسة نفيد بيها الناس . 
  
  محمد طه .

  Fun Arabic fact: when the verb is masculine and the subject is feminine such as (قال نسوة) which translates as (some women said), it means they are few. But if the verb is feminine and the subject is masculine such as (قالت الأعراب) which translates as (the "nomad" said), it means they are a lot.

  كتاب الإيمان1   Faith
  (1c)Chapter - Section 3(1c)باب - الفصل الثالث
  Mishkat al-Masabih 42
  Miqdad reported that he heard God’s messenger say, “There will not remain on the face of the earth a mud-brick house or a camel’s hair tent which God will not cause the confession of Islam to enter bringing both mighty honour and abject abasement. God will either honour the occupants and put them among its adherents, or will humiliate them and they will be subject to it.” Miqdad said, “God will then receive complete obedience.”
  
  Ahmad transmitted it.
  عَن الْمِقْدَاد بن الْأسود قَالَ: سَمِعْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: " يَقُولُ لَا يَبْقَى عَلَى ظَهْرِ الْأَرْضِ بَيْتُ مَدَرٍ وَلَا وَبَرٍ إِلَّا أَدْخَلَهُ اللَّهُ كلمة الاسلام بعز عَزِيز أَو ذل ذليل إِمَّا يعزهم الله عز وَجل فَيَجْعَلُهُمْ مِنْ أَهْلِهَا أَوْ يُذِلُّهُمْ فَيَدِينُونَ لَهَا رَوَاهُ أَحمد
